qs.q: A patient with schistosomiasis presents with terminal-stream urine. When is the best time to collect the urine sample for schistosoma eggs in endemic areas?
qs.e: Terminal-stream urine for schistosoma eggs should be collected around midday after exercise to optimize egg shedding. Early-morning samples are instead reserved for tuberculosis (AFB × 3).

qs.q: A patient with confirmed schistosomiasis causing terminal haematuria requires specific medical therapy. What is the correct drug and dose?
o: Albendazole 400 mg daily for three days
qs.e: Praziquantel 40 mg/kg as a single dose is the standard medical treatment for schistosomiasis. Antibiotics like ciprofloxacin are used for urinary tract infections rather than parasitic infestations.

qs.q: A patient living near a freshwater body is diagnosed with urinary schistosomiasis. In which specific venous plexus do the adult Schistosoma haematobium worms ultimately reside?
o: Vesical venous plexus of the bladder
Mesenteric veins of the small bowel
Bile ducts of the liver parenchyma
Mesenteric veins of the colon wall
qs.e: Adult Schistosoma haematobium worms mature and reside specifically in the bladder veins, leading to eggs in the urine. S. mansoni and S. japonicum inhabit mesenteric veins.

qs.q: In regions where urinary schistosomiasis is endemic, which bladder tumour type predominates?
qs.e: Schistosoma haematobium infection is strongly linked to squamous cell carcinoma. The other types are not the predominant lesion in this setting.
qs.s: Bladder Cancer & Urothelial Neoplasms: Types, Risks, Pathogenesis: MCQs

qs.q: A 45-year-old woman from an area endemic for urinary schistosomiasis presents with haematuria. Which histologic type of bladder carcinoma is most likely to be found?
qs.e: Squamous cell carcinoma is common in areas where urinary schistosomiasis is endemic, arising from chronic irritation and squamous metaplasia. Urothelial carcinoma is the most common type globally but not specifically linked to schistosomiasis.

qs.q: How is Schistosomiasis (Bilharzia) typically transmitted to humans?
o: Swallowing food contaminated with embryonated Ascaris eggs
The bite of infected mosquitoes transmitting sporozoites into blood
Ingestion of raw or undercooked beef containing encysted larvae
Direct skin penetration by parasites emerging from snails in fresh water
qs.e: Schistosoma directly penetrates the skin of people swimming in contaminated rivers and lakes where infected snails release the parasite. It is not acquired by ingestion of contaminated food.

qs.q: What is the primary cause of damage to the intestinal wall during intestinal Schistosomiasis?
o: Massive hemolysis resulting from red blood cell rupture by merozoites
Direct mechanical lacerations caused by adult worm mouth suckers
The host's inflammatory response to eggs deposited at that site
Nutrient depletion caused by large burdens of ribbon-shaped tapeworms
qs.e: Damage to the intestinal wall in intestinal Schistosomiasis is caused by the host's inflammatory response to eggs deposited at that site. The eggs also secrete proteolytic substances.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Schistosomiasis is a parasitic infection that can cause chronic liver, intestinal, or urogenital disease. Diagnosis relies on stool/urine eggs and serology, while treatment is praziquantel. Management focuses on parasite clearance and complication prevention.

sections.p: Schistosomiasis is caused by trematode worms of the genus Schistosoma. Transmission occurs when skin contacts contaminated freshwater. Diagnosis is confirmed by detecting eggs in stool or urine, supported by serology when eggs are scarce.

t.b: Detects S. mansoni or S. japonicum eggs; positive means active infection.
Detects S. haematobium eggs; positive indicates urogenital disease.
Positive indicates exposure; useful when eggs are not found.

sections.p: Severity is graded by parasite load and organ involvement. Mild disease shows few eggs and minimal symptoms. Moderate disease has moderate egg counts and organ dysfunction. Severe disease presents with high egg counts, portal hypertension, or bladder carcinoma risk.

The primary cause is contact with freshwater infested by Biomphalaria (S. mansoni), Bulinus (S. haematobium), or Oncomelania (S. japonicum) snails. Secondary factors include HIV, malaria, and malnutrition that worsen outcomes.
Early infection causes a Katayama fever with fever, cough, and eosinophilia. Chronic infection leads to abdominal pain, hepatosplenomegaly, portal hypertension, hematuria, or bladder lesions.
Investigations confirm infection, assess organ damage, and guide treatment. In low-resource settings, microscopy is primary; serology and imaging are adjuncts.

t.b: Elevated transaminases or bilirubin indicate hepatic involvement.
Detects periportal fibrosis or bladder wall thickening.
Assesses renal function if urogenital disease suspected.

sections.p: Complications can be life-threatening: portal hypertension with variceal bleeding, bladder carcinoma, severe anemia, or acute hepatic failure. Red flags include massive hematuria, upper GI bleeding, or sudden liver failure.

First-line therapy is praziquantel, chosen for its broad efficacy and low toxicity. Supportive care includes pain control, iron supplementation, and management of portal hypertension. Alternatives like oxamniquine are reserved for specific species.

t.b: Treats all Schistosoma species; reduces egg output.
Treat secondary bacterial infections if present.

sections.p: After treatment, repeat stool/urine exams after 4–6 weeks to confirm cure. Prevention focuses on avoiding freshwater contact, using protective footwear, and snail control.
Schistosomiasis can mimic other causes of portal hypertension such as viral hepatitis or alcoholic cirrhosis, and hematuria can be mistaken for urinary tract infection.
Egg counts may be falsely low in early infection or after treatment. Serology can remain positive long after cure, leading to overdiagnosis.
b: Low egg counts in early disease

faq.q: What is the most common symptom of chronic schistosomiasis?
faq.a: Abdominal pain and hepatosplenomegaly due to periportal fibrosis.
Yes, praziquantel effectively cures most infections, but reinfection is common without preventive measures.
Eosinophilia indicates a parasitic infection and supports the diagnosis when eggs are not seen.
